rows: Consistent with historical run rates; ~22% year-end marker (historical 23-24%)
Record Q1 revenue of ~$260M, up 95%; first time exceeding $200M in quarterly revenue and a 46% sequential gain over Q4 2022.
ACV reached a record 95.4% MULOC (from 69.5%) - far faster than the 12-18 months management internally expected; convenience ACV up 37.7 points to 93.4%.
Celsius is the #3 US energy drink at a record 7.5% share (doubled from 3.7%) and the #2 brand on Amazon.
Record non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA of $48.7M (>18% of sales), aided by sales/marketing timing benefits and SG&A operating leverage.
A ~$20-25M inventory build in the Pepsi mixing centers (incremental sales) was 'in large part' preparation for the summer selling season; expected to be sustained through summer.
Gross margin improvement was driven by lower average can prices and orbit-model leverage, partly offset by higher freight and a few million dollars of inventory write-offs.
Management expects mid-40s full-year gross margin with first-half pressure during distribution integration and back-half upside as the supply chain is optimized.
Items per store rose to 13.6 (recorded channel) from 8.6; management frames 15-17 by year-end as the path to a ~10% category share.
Summer 2023 is a key seasonal test - the '100 days of summer' marketing program with planned activation step-up in Q2/Q3.
The Q1 cash balance of ~$634M included ~$38M primarily due back to Pepsi (excess distributor-transition funds), to be returned in Q2.
International expansion targeted for early 2024 - a handful of bigger energy markets across Europe and APAC, not a 'spray and pray' approach; 2023 is a planning year.
Management committed to disclosing significant quarter-end mixing-center inventory deltas each quarter and emphasized scan data over sell-in.
Aluminum cans now sourced domestically, benefiting margins; capacity can quickly double via the orbit model and additional co-packers.
G&A rose 75% on a back-office build-out (finance/IT/legal); operating leverage expected as the company scales.

How do the spring resets look from a shelf-space standpoint - how much into existing energy doors vs new doors? Does Celsius still want legacy energy doors, and how much velocity strength is higher-velocity stores vs brand awareness?

The resets drove the biggest ACV gains in convenience (+37.7 points to 95.4% MULOC); items per store rose to 13.6 from 8.6. With ACV near 95%, the bigger opportunity is breadth within retailers - placements, cold availability, coolers. Legacy energy doors remain; new SKUs and summer flavors (lemon lime, green apple cherry at 7-Eleven) add breadth. Velocity is increasing with room to go, but no forward guidance.
Channel fill vs reorders & Q2 read-through
How much of the Q1 reacceleration was initial channel fill for new stores/doors/SKUs vs genuine reorders from sell-through, and what is the Q2 impact? What is the outlook for the convenience channel?

Distribution gains came with the resets; rising velocity is a strong sign Celsius is cycling through any pipe-fill - the Pepsi inventory increase was ~$20-25M (average quarterly impact). Celsius gained substantial Tier 3/Tier 4 convenience distribution since October; management is confident in convenience. Food service (~10% of Pepsi business) shows broad consumer resonance.
Path to 10% market share & competitive launches
Given the ACV progress, what is now possible in the Pepsi system - the 10% share ambition looks near-term? How worrisome are recent competitive launches (Monster Zero Sugar, Rainstorm, Prime)?

Management is amazed at the pace of the ACV ramp (~95%, far faster than the expected 12-18 months); needs a quarter or two to learn portfolio performance in newly expanded convenience. Gaining 15-17 items per store by year-end (from 13.6) is the path to a ~10% category share. The energy category is fiercely competitive with constant entrants; declined to comment on specific brands, citing runway (Miami-Fort Lauderdale ~21.7% share, #2 on Amazon).

How much did the inventory write-off impact Q1 gross margin, and what does 'first-half pressure' mean (vs mid-40s or YoY)? What work informs the international decision, which markets, and is the rollout broad-based or gradual?

The Q4-to-Q1 margin movement was driven by a couple million dollars of inventory write-offs (supply-chain build-out) and slightly higher freight; back half sees freight-lane cleanup, confident in mid-40s with back-half upside. The international rollout targets well-defined energy markets in Europe and APAC - a handful first to learn, mostly partnering with Pepsi; 2024 the launch year, 2023 the planning year.
Was foodservice 10% of sales and what was its Q1 pipe-fill? Is the ~$45M scan-vs-reported gap (138% Q1 scan growth) a consistent lag similar to the ~$50M Q4 gap?

Foodservice is ~10% of Pepsi sales (not total sales); it is not a pipe-fill but momentum built since October, with good reorders and large opportunity in eateries and fast-casual. The scan gap reflects register sell-through with lumpiness through the Pepsi value chain (mixing centers, sales barns, customers) plus the mix of slower-growing Amazon and club businesses and some timing.
Supply chain capacity & club channel status
Can the supply chain continue servicing demand long-term, particularly the domestically-sourced aluminum can supply? Where are the 18-pack transition, second variety pack, and BJ's rollout?

Raw materials are in great shape with multiple US can partners; capacity can quickly double via the orbit model, additional co-packers and existing co-packer capacity. The 18-pack transition is 'pretty much' complete across all club channels, the core variety pack is expanding with incremental Vibe-pack placements; both packs perform well, with room for further flavors and single flavors.
Mixing-center build composition & SG&A run rate

Is the $20-25M mixing-center build largely an adjustment to faster sell-through (a reset to higher normalized levels) or volume pulled forward? How does SG&A run rate look over the rest of the year given the marketing step-up vs operating leverage?

The build is 'in large part' preparation for the summer selling season and planned activations - partly anticipation of Q2/Q3. The plan is to maintain the historical run rate (S&M ~23-24%); Q1 came in at just over 18% (helped by the inventory build and revenue-growth leverage); summer marketing/sales spend increases, with a year-end goal around a 22% marker.

Is the back-office buildout sufficient for the near term given summer launches and the international transition, or will the company keep building through 2023? What is the branded cooler count and progress penetrating the ~50,000 Pepsi energy coolers?

Celsius has built a strong finance/IT/GL/legal team with a few more hires planned, plus continued investment in operations, sales and marketing; leverage opportunities expected especially in HR and marketing now ACV is at 95%; international entry needs initial investment. Celsius decided not to disclose the specific cooler count going forward, citing competitive sensitivity, though it still has a big cooler push.
